references.authors: Bordewijk EM, Wang R, Askie LM, et al.
references.title: Data integrity of 35 randomised controlled trials in women' health
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: Of 35 women's-health RCTs published 2006-2016 by two authors from one institute, 26 shared many similar baseline and outcome values, and baseline distributions were unlikely to reflect proper randomisation.

references.authors: Bordewijk EM, Wang R, van Wely M, et al.
references.title: To share or not to share data: how valid are trials evaluating first-line ovulation induction for polycystic ovary syndrome?
references.finding: In PCOS ovulation-induction trials, RCTs that did not share individual data had more risk of bias (75% vs 24% not low risk), no adequate registration, more statistical problems and different pooled effects than trials that shared data.

references.authors: Li W, van Wely M, Gurrin L, et al.
references.title: Integrity of randomized controlled trials: challenges and solutions
references.finding: Review from the Monash group: compromised RCT integrity undermines systematic reviews; data can be checked via summary statistics and individual participant data, and reviewers should account for problematic trials.

references.authors: Mol BW, Bordewijk EM, Rogozińska E, et al.
references.title: Data integrity of 14 randomised controlled trials
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: Integrity check of 14 RCTs by one Egyptian author (2004-2019): duplicated baseline tables, plagiarism and baseline p-values implying non-random allocation; unretracted trials should not inform practice until investigated.

references.authors: Carlisle JB
references.title: False individual patient data and zombie randomised controlled trials submitted to Anaesthesia
references.finding: Of 526 RCTs submitted to Anaesthesia, 14% had false data and 8% were 'zombie' trials; when individual patient data were requested, 44% had false data and 26% were zombies.

references.authors: Wilkinson J, Heal C, Antoniou GA, et al.
references.title: Assessing the feasibility and impact of clinical trial trustworthiness checks via an application to Cochrane Reviews: Stage 2 of the INSPECT-SR project
references.finding: Applying 72 trustworthiness checks to RCTs in 50 Cochrane reviews raised some or serious concerns about authenticity for 25% and 6% of trials; removing them left 22% of meta-analyses empty, and concerns were unrelated to Risk-of-Bias or GRADE ratings.

references.authors: Zou H, Abdallah KS, Wirleitner B, et al.
references.title: Intrauterine human chorionic gonadotropin administration before embryo transfer (IHABT): an individual participant data meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.n: 7 RCTs with IPD, 2244 women (28 RCTs found)
references.finding: IPD meta-analysis: intrauterine hCG before embryo transfer did not improve live birth (OR 0.99, 0.83-1.19); all 7 IPD trials passed trustworthiness checks, none of the trials without IPD did, and those untrustworthy trials produced the apparent benefit.

references.authors: Papaleo E, Unfer V, Baillargeon JP, et al.
references.title: RETRACTED: Myo-inositol may improve oocyte quality in intracytoplasmic sperm injection cycles. A prospective, controlled, randomized trial
references.finding: RETRACTED (2025) myo-inositol ICSI trial; retracted at the request of the ASRM Publications Committee after an undisclosed conflict of interest with the supplement maker was reported. Cited only to flag it.

references.title: Retraction notice to 'Myo-inositol may improve oocyte quality in intracytoplasmic sperm injection cycles. A prospective, controlled, randomized trial' [Fertility and Sterility 91 (2009) 1750-1754]
references.finding: Retraction notice (Fertil Steril 2025) for Papaleo 2009 myo-inositol RCT.

references.authors: Pacchiarotti A, Carlomagno G, Antonini G, et al.
references.title: Effect of myo-inositol and melatonin versus myo-inositol, in a randomized controlled trial, for improving in vitro fertilization of patients with polycystic ovarian syndrome
references.finding: RETRACTED myo-inositol plus melatonin IVF RCT in PCOS (already flagged on the site). Cited only to flag it.

references.authors: Kotb MM, Hassan AM, AwadAllah AM
references.title: Does dehydroepiandrosterone improve pregnancy rate in women undergoing IVF/ICSI with expected poor ovarian response according to the Bologna criteria? A randomized controlled trial
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: RETRACTED (2026) Egyptian RCT of DHEA in poor responders undergoing IVF/ICSI. Cited only to flag it.

references.authors: Kotb MMM, Hassan AMA, AwadAllah AMA
references.title: Retraction notice to "Does Dehydroepiandrosterone improve pregnancy rate in women undergoing IVF/ICSI with expected poor ovarian response according to the Bologna criteria? A randomized controlled trial" [Eur. J. Obstet. Gynecol. Reprod. Biol. 200 (2016) 11-15]
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: Retraction notice (Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol 2026) for the Kotb 2016 DHEA RCT.

references.authors: Elprince M, Kishk EA, Metawie OM, et al.
references.title: Ovarian stimulation after dehydroepiandrosterone supplementation in poor ovarian reserve: a randomized clinical trial
references.finding: RETRACTED (2024) RCT of DHEA before ovarian stimulation in poor ovarian reserve. Cited only to flag it.

references.authors: El Refaeey A, Selem A, Badawy A
references.title: Combined coenzyme Q10 and clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction in clomiphene-citrate-resistant polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: RETRACTED (2023, after an expression of concern) RCT of CoQ10 plus clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant PCOS. Cited only to flag it.

references.authors: El Sharkwy IA, Abd El Aziz WM
references.title: Randomized controlled trial of N-acetylcysteine versus l-carnitine among women with clomiphene-citrate-resistant polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: RETRACTED RCT of N-acetylcysteine vs L-carnitine in clomiphene-resistant PCOS; it was the only source for two outcomes in the Cochrane female-antioxidant review. Cited only to flag it.

references.authors: Maged AM, Rashwan H, AbdelAziz S, et al.
references.title: Randomized controlled trial of the effect of endometrial injury on implantation and clinical pregnancy rates during the first ICSI cycle
references.finding: RETRACTED (2024) Egyptian RCT reporting higher implantation and pregnancy with endometrial injury before first ICSI. Cited only to flag it.

references.authors: Helmy MEE, Maher MA, Elkhouly NI, et al.
references.title: A randomized trial of local endometrial injury during ovulation induction cycles
references.finding: RETRACTED (2024) Egyptian RCT of endometrial injury during clomiphene ovulation-induction cycles. Cited only to flag it.

references.authors: de Ligny WR, de Bruin JP, Smits RM, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant Treatment and the Chance to Conceive in Men Seeking Fertility Care: The SUMMER Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: SUMMER (21 Dutch centres): 6 months of an antioxidant/B-vitamin supplement vs placebo did not raise ongoing pregnancy (33.8% vs 37.5%; aOR 0.85, 0.66-1.09); in the 4-6 month window it was lower (15.5% vs 21.5%); no effect on semen or SDF.

references.authors: Schisterman EF, Sjaarda LA, Clemons T, et al.
references.title: Effect of Folic Acid and Zinc Supplementation in Men on Semen Quality and Live Birth Among Couples Undergoing Infertility Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: FAZST: folic acid 5 mg plus zinc 30 mg in male partners did not change live birth (34% vs 35%) or semen quality, and slightly raised DNA fragmentation (29.7% vs 27.2%).

references.authors: Steiner AZ, Hansen KR, Barnhart KT, et al.
references.title: The effect of antioxidants on male factor infertility: the Males, Antioxidants, and Infertility (MOXI) randomized clinical trial
references.finding: MOXI: a 7-ingredient antioxidant did not improve semen parameters or DNA fragmentation at 3 months; cumulative live birth 15% vs 24% with placebo (not significant).

references.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
references.finding: Cochrane 2022: antioxidants for male subfertility may raise live birth but the evidence is very low certainty and driven by small trials at high risk of bias.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Cannarella R, Saleh R, et al.
references.title: Impact of Antioxidant Therapy on Natural Pregnancy Outcomes and Semen Parameters in Infertile Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
references.finding: Meta-analysis by Agarwal's group: antioxidants associated with higher spontaneous pregnancy and better semen parameters, but no effect on live birth (4 studies) or SDF (3 studies).

references.authors: Szabó A, Váncsa S, Hegyi P, et al.
references.title: Assessing the efficacy of varicocelectomy, antioxidants, FSH treatment, and lifestyle modifications on sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: SDF fell 6.7 points 3 months after varicocelectomy (12.4 at 6 months), about 4.3 points with antioxidants, 6.7 with FSH and 3.2 with lifestyle change; authors judged antioxidants 'questionable'.

references.authors: Melhem SJ, Melhem M, Haddad R, et al.
references.title: Pharmacologic and Nutritional Therapies in Idiopathic Male Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Antioxidants were associated with higher sperm concentration and motility in idiopathic infertility, but certainty was very low, heterogeneity >80% and prediction intervals crossed zero; live-birth data lacking.

references.authors: Szabó A, Váncsa S, Hegyi P, et al.
references.title: Lifestyle-, environmental-, and additional health factors associated with an increased sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: SDF risk factors: varicocele +13.6 points, smoking +9.2, age over 50 +12.6; Chlamydia and HPV effects negligible; abstinence period showed no significant SDF difference.

references.authors: Esteves SC, Roque M, Bradley CK, et al.
references.title: Reproductive outcomes of testicular versus ejaculated sperm for intracytoplasmic sperm injection among men with high levels of DNA fragmentation in semen: systematic review and meta-analysis
references.n: 5 studies (143 men) paired SDF; 4 studies (507 cycles)
references.finding: Testicular sperm had about 25 points lower SDF than ejaculated sperm, and Testi-ICSI was associated with higher pregnancy and live birth in men with high SDF (non-randomised data).

references.authors: Khoo CC, Cayetano-Alcaraz AA, Rashid R, et al.
references.title: Does Testicular Sperm Improve Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection Outcomes for Nonazoospermic Infertile Men with Elevated Sperm DNA Fragmentation? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
references.finding: Testicular sperm associated with higher pregnancy (OR 2.51) and live birth (OR 2.59, SCSA studies) in high-SDF men, but evidence quality was too low to recommend it outside trials.

references.authors: Hozyen M, Hasanen E, Elqusi K, et al.
references.title: Reproductive Outcomes of Different Sperm Selection Techniques for ICSI Patients with Abnormal Sperm DNA Fragmentation: a Randomized Controlled Trial
references.finding: Egyptian 4-arm RCT in high-SDF ICSI: testicular sperm gave lower cleavage, blastulation and top-blastocyst rates than ejaculated-sperm methods; PICSI and MACS had the highest ongoing pregnancy.

references.authors: Mantravadi KC, Rao D
references.title: In cases with raised sperm DNA fragmentation, can sperm selection by magnetic-activated cell sorting or testicular sperm aspiration help improve reproductive outcomes?
references.finding: Small Indian RCT in high-SDF couples with failed IVF: TESA and MACS gave similar live birth; no ejaculated-sperm control arm.

references.authors: Romano M, Cirillo F, Spadaro D, et al.
references.title: High sperm DNA fragmentation: do we have robust evidence to support antioxidants and testicular sperm extraction to improve fertility outcomes? a narrative review
references.finding: Narrative review: evidence for antioxidants or testicular sperm in high SDF is non-conclusive because of small samples and risk of bias.

references.authors: Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA)
references.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation: treatment add-on rating
references.finding: HFEA (page updated 24 Sep 2026): after SDF testing, antioxidants and sperm selection rated grey; TESE/TESA with ICSI rated RED for male-factor infertility (insufficient evidence plus procedural risk).

references.authors: Persad E, O'Loughlin CA, Kaur S, et al.
references.title: Surgical or radiological treatment for varicoceles in subfertile men
references.finding: Cochrane 2021: uncertain whether varicocele treatment improves live birth (2 studies, RR 2.27, 0.19-26.6); treatment may improve pregnancy.

references.authors: Palani A, Cannarella R, Saleh R, et al.
references.title: Impact of Varicocele Repair on Assisted Reproductive Technique Outcomes in Infertile Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Men who had varicocele repair before ICSI had higher fertilisation, clinical pregnancy (OR 1.38) and live birth (OR 2.07) than unrepaired men; all studies observational.

references.authors: Murugesu S, Kasaven LS, Petrie A, et al.
references.title: Does advanced paternal age affect outcomes following assisted reproductive technology? A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Paternal age under 40 associated with higher clinical pregnancy and live birth in autologous IVF; under 50 with lower miscarriage and more blastocysts in donor-egg cycles where maternal age is controlled.

references.authors: Begon E, Lefebvre T, Arbo E, et al.
references.title: Does paternal age affect the live birth rate in donor oocyte cycles? A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: In egg-donation cycles live birth fell slightly but linearly with paternal age, with no threshold.

references.authors: Kong A, Frigge ML, Masson G, et al.
references.title: Rate of de novo mutations and the importance of father's age to disease risk
references.finding: De novo mutations rise by about two per year of father's age (doubling about every 16.5 years); father's age explains most variation in de novo mutation counts.

references.authors: D'Onofrio BM, Rickert ME, Frans E, et al.
references.title: Paternal age at childbearing and offspring psychiatric and academic morbidity
references.finding: Sibling- and cousin-comparison designs found paternal-age associations with autism, psychosis, bipolar disorder and academic problems as large or larger than population estimates, consistent with a causal mutation pathway.

references.authors: Khandwala YS, Baker VL, Shaw GM, et al.
references.title: Association of paternal age with perinatal outcomes between 2007 and 2016 in the United States: population based cohort study
references.finding: Fathers 45+ had 14% higher odds of preterm birth and partners 34% higher odds of gestational diabetes after adjustment for maternal age; population impact modest.

references.authors: Levine H, Jørgensen N, Martino-Andrade A, et al.
references.title: Temporal trends in sperm count: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis of samples collected globally in the 20th and 21st centuries
references.finding: Updated global meta-regression: mean sperm concentration among unselected men fell 51.6% between 1973 and 2018, with the decline appearing to steepen in recent decades.

references.authors: Boulicault M, Perret M, Galka J, et al.
references.title: The future of sperm: a biovariability framework for understanding global sperm count trends
references.finding: Critique of the sperm-count-decline hypothesis: proposes that sperm count varies widely and non-pathologically, and that trends need ecological and life-history interpretation rather than a decline narrative.

references.authors: Steiner AZ, Pritchard D, Stanczyk FZ, et al.
references.title: Association Between Biomarkers of Ovarian Reserve and Infertility Among Older Women of Reproductive Age
references.finding: Low AMH (<0.7 ng/mL) was not associated with lower probability of conceiving by 6 or 12 cycles (84% vs 75% by 12 cycles).

references.authors: Harris BS, Jukic AM, Truong T, et al.
references.title: Markers of ovarian reserve as predictors of future fertility
references.finding: Diminished ovarian reserve (AMH <0.7 or FSH >=10) was not associated with lower future live birth, infertility or fecundability.

references.authors: Nelson SM, Shaw M, Ewing BJ, et al.
references.title: Antimüllerian hormone levels are associated with time to pregnancy in a cohort study of 3,150 women
references.finding: In the largest TTP cohort (buyers of a commercial hormone test), AMH <1 ng/mL was associated with modestly lower conception (adjHR 0.77, 0.64-0.94); peak per-cycle probability 11% vs 14%.

references.authors: Peigné M, Bernard V, Dijols L, et al.
references.title: Using serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels to predict the chance of live birth after spontaneous or assisted conception: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: AMH relates non-linearly to cumulative live birth after IVF/ICSI, with no threshold below which live birth is impossible; data lacking for natural conception.

references.authors: Hirsch A, Hirsh Raccah B, Rotem R, et al.
references.title: Planned oocyte cryopreservation: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis
references.finding: Planned egg freezing: 11% returned to use eggs; live birth per returning patient 28% overall, 52% if frozen at 35 or younger and 19% at 40+.

references.authors: Kirubarajan A, Patel P, Thangavelu N, et al.
references.title: Return rates and pregnancy outcomes after oocyte preservation for planned fertility delay: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Return rate after planned egg freezing 10.8% (median 7-year follow-up); live birth in 28.9% of those who thawed eggs.

references.authors: Cascante SD, Grifo JA, Licciardi F, et al.
references.title: The effects of age, mature oocyte number, and cycle number on cumulative live birth rates after planned oocyte cryopreservation
references.finding: Cumulative live birth 43% overall and >70% with >=20 mature eggs frozen before 38; age and number of eggs, not number of cycles, predicted success.

references.authors: Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA)
references.title: Treatment add-ons with limited evidence (HFEA add-ons rating list)
references.finding: HFEA add-on ratings for 'chances of having a baby' (page reviewed 28 Sep 2026): yellow for endometrial scratching, hyaluronate transfer medium, elective freeze-all; grey for assisted hatching, androgens, intralipids, IMSI, intrauterine culture, microbiome testing, SDF; black for time-lapse and PICSI; red for endometrial receptivity testing, IVIG, steroids, PRP and PGT-A. No green.

references.authors: ESHRE Add-ons working group, Lundin K, Bentzen JG, et al.
references.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine†
references.finding: ESHRE 2023: 42 recommendations on add-ons; none based on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence.

references.authors: Yan J, Qin Y, Zhao H, et al.
references.title: Live Birth with or without Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Aneuploidy
references.finding: Among women with >=3 good blastocysts, cumulative live birth was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% with conventional IVF (non-inferiority of conventional IVF shown).

references.authors: Lin X, Wu D, Zhang C, et al.
references.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy versus no genetic testing in couples undergoing intracytoplasmic sperm injection for severe male infertility: multicentre, open label, randomised controlled trial
references.finding: BMJ RCT in severe male factor ICSI: PGT-A did not change cumulative live birth (60.4% vs 60.9%) but lowered pregnancy loss after first transfer (5.8% vs 19.1%).

references.authors: Practice Committees of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology. Electronic address: asrm@asrm.org
references.title: The use of preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy: a committee opinion
references.finding: ASRM 2024: value of PGT-A as routine screening for all IVF patients has not been demonstrated; multicentre RCTs found similar outcomes; miscarriage benefit unclear.

references.authors: Mumusoglu S, Telek SB, Ata B
references.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy in unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: In unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss, low-quality evidence suggests PGT-A lowers pregnancy loss and raises live birth per transfer and per patient; RCTs needed.

references.authors: Beebeejaun Y, Bakalova D, Mania A, et al.
references.title: Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Aneuploidy Versus Morphological Selection in Women Aged 35-42: Results of a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
references.finding: Pilot RCT in women 35-42: PGT-A vs morphology gave cumulative live birth 72% vs 52% after up to three single transfers (not significant; feasibility trial).

references.authors: Heymann D, Vidal L, Or Y, et al.
references.title: Hyaluronic acid in embryo transfer media for assisted reproductive technologies
references.finding: Cochrane 2020: hyaluronan (0.5 mg/mL) transfer medium probably raises live birth (RR 1.21, moderate certainty); miscarriage benefit not seen in low-risk-of-bias trials.

references.authors: Rocha RM, Andrade MCR, Barcelos IDES, et al.
references.title: Hyaluronic Acid Enriched Medium for Embryo Transfer: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
references.finding: Hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium: live birth RR 1.14 (0.99-1.31, NS), 1.06 (0.85-1.31) after excluding high-risk-of-bias trials; certainty very low.

references.authors: Arian SE, Hessami K, Khatibi A, et al.
references.title: Endometrial receptivity array before frozen embryo transfer cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: ERA before frozen transfer did not change live birth or ongoing pregnancy (OR 1.38, 0.79-2.41).

references.authors: Wilkinson J, Stocking K
references.title: Some common, fatal flaws in systematic reviews of observational studies
references.finding: Uses ERA systematic reviews as an example of common fatal flaws in meta-analyses of observational studies (critical appraisal and pooling errors).

references.authors: Doyle N, Jahandideh S, Hill MJ, et al.
references.title: Effect of Timing by Endometrial Receptivity Testing vs Standard Timing of Frozen Embryo Transfer on Live Birth in Patients Undergoing In Vitro Fertilization: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: Receptivity-timed vs standard frozen euploid transfer: live birth 58.5% vs 61.9% (RR 0.95, NS).

references.authors: Sun Y, Cui L, Lu Y, et al.
references.title: Prednisone vs Placebo and Live Birth in Patients With Recurrent Implantation Failure Undergoing In Vitro Fertilization: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: JAMA RCT in recurrent implantation failure: prednisone did not improve live birth (37.8% vs 38.8%) and increased biochemical loss (17.3% vs 9.9%) and preterm delivery (11.8% vs 5.5%).

references.authors: Boomsma CM, Kamath MS, Keay SD, et al.
references.title: Peri-implantation glucocorticoid administration for assisted reproductive technology cycles
references.finding: Cochrane 2022: uncertain whether peri-implantation glucocorticoids improve live birth (OR 1.37, 0.69-2.71; very low certainty).

references.authors: Dang VQ, Vuong LN, Luu TM, et al.
references.title: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection versus conventional in-vitro fertilisation in couples with infertility in whom the male partner has normal total sperm count and motility: an open-label, randomised controlled trial
references.finding: With normal semen, ICSI vs conventional IVF: live birth 35% vs 31% (RR 1.11, NS); fertilisation failure 5% vs 6%.

references.authors: Fancsovits P, Lehner A, Kaszas Z, et al.
references.title: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection does not improve the outcome of IVF treatments in patients with advanced maternal age or low oocyte number: A randomized controlled trial
references.finding: In women >=40 and/or with <=4 oocytes (non-severe male factor), ICSI gave lower fertilisation (53% vs 62%) and no better live birth than conventional IVF; worse with both age and few eggs.

references.authors: Naik S, Lepine S, Nagels HE, et al.
references.title: Androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone or testosterone) for women undergoing assisted reproduction
references.finding: Cochrane 2024: DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth (OR 1.30, 0.95-1.76, moderate certainty); testosterone likely improves it (OR 2.53).

references.authors: Conforti A, Carbone L, Di Girolamo R, et al.
references.title: Therapeutic management in women with a diminished ovarian reserve: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: In POSEIDON-defined diminished ovarian reserve, testosterone was the only adjuvant associated with higher live birth (OR 2.19).

references.authors: Etrusco A, Agrifoglio V, Castillo Farfán JC, et al.
references.title: Effectiveness of hormone add-on strategies in ovarian stimulation for women with poor ovarian response: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Network meta-analysis of hormonal add-ons in poor responders: no significant live-birth differences among add-ons (very low evidence); growth hormone ranked best for oocyte numbers.

references.authors: Sood A, Mohiyiddeen G, Ahmad G, et al.
references.title: Growth hormone for in vitro fertilisation (IVF)
references.finding: Cochrane 2021: growth hormone slightly increases oocytes and pregnancy in poor responders; effect on live birth uncertain (low to very low certainty).

references.authors: Norman RJ, Alvino H, Hull LM, et al.
references.title: Human growth hormone for poor responders: a randomized placebo-controlled trial provides no evidence for improved live birth rate
references.finding: LIGHT: growth hormone vs placebo in poor responders, live birth 14.5% vs 13.7%; stopped short of planned size.

references.authors: Craciunas L, Tsampras N, Raine-Fenning N, et al.
references.title: Intrauterine administration of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) for subfertile women undergoing assisted reproduction
references.finding: Cochrane 2018: intrauterine hCG >=500 IU before cleavage-stage transfer improved live birth (moderate quality); no evidence for blastocyst transfer; most trials at high risk of bias.

references.authors: Perera AK, Gan J, Afroz A, et al.
references.title: Endometrial injury in women undergoing in vitro fertilisation (IVF)
references.finding: Cochrane 2026, restricted to low-risk-of-bias trials: effect of endometrial injury on live birth unclear (OR 1.12, 0.98-1.28).

references.authors: Lensen S, Osavlyuk D, Armstrong S, et al.
references.title: A Randomized Trial of Endometrial Scratching before In Vitro Fertilization
references.finding: PIP trial: live birth 26.1% with and without endometrial scratching.

references.authors: Bhide P, Chan DYL, Lanz D, et al.
references.title: Clinical effectiveness and safety of time-lapse imaging systems for embryo incubation and selection in in-vitro fertilisation treatment (TILT): a multicentre, three-parallel-group, double-blind, randomised controlled trial
references.finding: TILT: live birth 33.7% time-lapse, 36.6% undisturbed culture, 33.0% standard care; no significant differences.

references.authors: Lacey L, Hassan S, Franik S, et al.
references.title: Assisted hatching on assisted conception (in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI))
references.finding: Cochrane 2021: assisted hatching has uncertain effect on live birth (OR 1.09, 0.92-1.29) and may raise multiple pregnancy.

references.authors: Vaidakis D, Papapanou M, Siristatidis CS
references.title: Autologous platelet-rich plasma for assisted reproduction
references.finding: Cochrane 2024: effect of intrauterine or intraovarian PRP uncertain; only one trial at low risk of bias, which showed no clear live-birth effect (OR 1.10, 0.38-3.14).

references.authors: Herlihy NS, Cakiroglu Y, Whitehead C, et al.
references.title: Effect of intraovarian platelet-rich plasma injection on IVF outcomes in women with poor ovarian response: the PROVA randomized controlled trial
references.finding: PROVA RCT: intraovarian PRP did not improve mature oocyte yield or other IVF outcomes in poor responders under 38.

references.authors: Miller D, Pavitt S, Sharma V, et al.
references.title: Physiological, hyaluronan-selected intracytoplasmic sperm injection for infertility treatment (HABSelect): a parallel, two-group, randomised trial
references.finding: HABSelect: PICSI vs ICSI term live birth 27.4% vs 25.2% (NS).

references.authors: Garg A, Nakhla O, Steeper M, et al.
references.title: Advanced sperm selection techniques for assisted reproduction
references.finding: Cochrane 2026: hyaluronan-selected ICSI may make little or no difference to live birth (RR 1.09) and probably slightly reduces miscarriage (RR 0.59); other selection methods very low certainty.

references.authors: Showell MG, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Jordan V, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for female subfertility
references.finding: Cochrane 2020 female antioxidants; March 2026 editorial note: 7 included trials retracted and 2 under expression of concern; editors judged their removal does not meaningfully change conclusions, but the El Sharkwy 2019 head-to-head data disappear.

references.authors: Showell MG, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Jordan V, et al.
references.title: Inositol for subfertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: Cochrane 2018: uncertain whether myo-inositol improves live birth in PCOS IVF (OR 2.42, 0.75-7.83); apparent miscarriage reduction driven by one trial with an unusually high control miscarriage rate.

references.authors: Zhang J, Zhang H, Zhou W, et al.
references.title: Effect of myo-inositol supplementation in mixed ovarian response IVF cohort: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Myo-inositol associated with higher MII oocyte rate in PCOS IVF but not in poor responders; surrogate outcomes.

audit.claim: Combination 'male fertility' antioxidants have at best weak, biased evidence; the best RCT (MOXI) found no gain in semen, DNA fragmentation or live birth.
audit.biases: Small single-centre trials at high risk of bias, surrogate outcomes (semen parameters, seminal MDA) instead of live birth, industry-made products, and research-integrity problems in the trial base: Cochrane's apparent live-birth gain disappears when high-risk-of-bias trials are removed [afert-deligny2022], and trustworthiness checks of Cochrane-included RCTs flag about a quarter for authenticity concerns that Risk-of-Bias tools do not catch [afert-wilkinson2025]. Positive meta-analyses come from groups with long-standing advocacy for antioxidant therapy and mostly report pregnancy rather than live birth [afert-agarwal2023].
audit.newer_evidence: Two large placebo-controlled trials have since reported. FAZST (2020, 2370 men): folic acid plus zinc did not change live birth (34% vs 35%) or semen quality and slightly raised DNA fragmentation [afert-schisterman2020]. SUMMER (2025, 1171 men, 21 Dutch centres): 6 months of an antioxidant/B-vitamin product did not raise ongoing pregnancy (33.8% vs 37.5%) and pregnancy was lower in the 4-6 month window when any effect should appear (15.5% vs 21.5%) [afert-deligny2025]. These confirm MOXI (live birth 15% vs 24%) [afert-steiner2020]. On the other side, a 2023 meta-analysis of 45 RCTs reports higher spontaneous pregnancy but no live-birth or SDF effect [afert-agarwal2023]; 2025-2026 meta-analyses find small SDF falls (about 4 points) and better semen numbers but at very low certainty with prediction intervals crossing zero [afert-szabo2025, afert-melhem2026]. HFEA rates antioxidants after SDF testing grey [afert-hfea2026sdf].
audit.bottom_line: The three largest, best-run trials (MOXI, FAZST, SUMMER) all found no live-birth benefit from male supplements, and two hinted at harm. Treat them as unproven and not worth paying for to improve fertility.

site_change.headline: Three large placebo-controlled RCTs (MOXI 2020, FAZST 2020 with 2370 men, SUMMER 2025 with 1171 men) found no gain in live birth or pregnancy from male antioxidant/vitamin supplements; SUMMER saw fewer pregnancies in months 4-6 (15.5% vs 21.5%).
site_change.note: Direction should be 'neutral' (or 'mixed' only for surrogate semen markers). Fill the empty debate field with Agarwal 2023 / Szabo 2025 vs MOXI, FAZST and SUMMER. Note that FAZST raised DFI slightly (29.7% vs 27.2%).

audit.claim: Testicular sperm carry about 25 points less DNA fragmentation, and pooled studies show higher pregnancy and live birth with ICSI in men with high ejaculated SDF.
audit.biases: Confounding by indication and selection: the pooled data are non-randomised comparisons in couples chosen after failed cycles, often from the same centres that promote the technique, and with regression to the mean in SDF [afert-esteves2017, afert-khoo2024]. Lower SDF in the sample is a surrogate; testicular sperm may carry more aneuploidy.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 studies (>536 men) found higher pregnancy (OR 2.51) and live birth (OR 2.59) but judged the evidence too weak to recommend outside trials [afert-khoo2024]. The only multi-arm RCT that included a testicular arm (Hozyen 2022, 302 couples) found testicular sperm gave lower cleavage, blastulation and top-blastocyst rates, with PICSI and MACS ejaculated-sperm arms doing best [afert-hozyen2022]. A small RCT found TESA and MACS similar but lacked an untreated control [afert-mantravadi2024]. Reviews call the evidence non-conclusive [afert-romano2023]. The HFEA now rates TESE/TESA with ICSI after SDF testing RED (insufficient evidence plus surgical risk) [afert-hfea2026sdf].
audit.bottom_line: Testicular sperm do have less fragmented DNA, but whether that means more babies is unproven; the one randomised comparison did not favour it and the UK regulator rates it red. It is a last-resort option for selected couples, ideally within a trial.

site_change.headline: Testicular sperm have about 25 points less DNA fragmentation, and non-randomised studies report more live births with ICSI, but the only randomised comparison did not favour it and the HFEA rates it red; consider only after other causes are fixed.
site_change.note: Add the HFEA red rating (Sep 2026) and the Hozyen 2022 RCT to debate; the current debate field says 'None'.

audit.claim: A palpable varicocele is the largest common driver of high SDF, adding roughly 10-14 points.
audit.biases: Cross-sectional comparisons in men attending infertility clinics (selection into care: men with varicocele and normal fertility are rarely tested); detection depends on examination; varicocele correlates with age and duration.
audit.newer_evidence: The 2023 risk-factor meta-analysis of 190 studies confirmed varicocele as the largest SDF association (+13.6 points) [afert-szabo2023]. Before-after data show SDF falls after repair (about 6.7 points at 3 months, 12.4 at 6 months), with a dose-response by grade, which supports causation [afert-szabo2025].
audit.bottom_line: The varicocele-SDF link holds and repair lowers SDF, which supports a causal role; the open question is how much that changes live birth (see varicocele-repair).

audit.claim: Repairing a clinical varicocele lowers SDF by about 7 points, more when SDF starts high; pregnancy benefit less certain.
audit.biases: SDF studies are before-after without untreated controls (regression to the mean, since men are selected for high SDF); ART-outcome studies compare men who chose repair with men who did not (confounding by indication, healthy-user).
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 86 studies found SDF fell 6.7 points at 3 months and 12.4 at 6 months after varicocelectomy, larger in grade II-III [afert-szabo2025]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 9 observational studies linked repair before ICSI with higher live birth (OR 2.07) [afert-palani2025], but Cochrane 2021 remains uncertain about live birth from randomised data (RR 2.27, 0.19-26.6) [afert-persad2021].
audit.bottom_line: The SDF drop is consistent; a live-birth gain is plausible but still rests mostly on non-randomised data.

site_change.note: Cite Szabo 2025 (SDF -6.7 at 3 months, -12.4 at 6 months) and Palani 2025 (observational ICSI live birth OR 2.07) in debate, alongside Cochrane's uncertainty; debate field currently 'None'.

audit.claim: SDF rises with age with a clear jump after 50 (+12.6 points), alongside more new mutations in offspring.
audit.biases: Older fathers differ in health, weight, varicocele duration and partner age (residual confounding by maternal age in IVF data); offspring-outcome associations can reflect parental psychiatric traits that delay parenthood.
audit.newer_evidence: Designs that control for confounding support a real effect. De novo mutations rise by about two per year of paternal age [afert-kong2012]. Swedish sibling comparisons (2.6 million births) found paternal-age associations with autism, psychosis and bipolar disorder as large as or larger than population estimates [afert-donofrio2014]. In donor-egg cycles, where egg age is fixed, live birth falls slightly and linearly with paternal age [afert-begon2023]; a 2022 meta-analysis of 32,484 cycles links paternal age over 40-50 to lower live birth and more miscarriage [afert-murugesu2022]. US birth data show 14% higher odds of preterm birth for fathers 45+ after adjusting for maternal age, with a modest population impact [afert-khandwala2018].
audit.bottom_line: Male age matters, with effects that are real but small for any single child; it adds to, and is much smaller than, the effect of female age.

site_change.note: Debate field says 'None': add the donor-egg (Begon 2023) and sibling-comparison (D'Onofrio 2014) evidence that supports causation, and that absolute risks stay small.

audit.claim: Female age is the dominant driver of egg quality; women with no euploid embryo rise from 2-6% (26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.
audit.biases: Embryo-biopsy data come from IVF patients (selection), but the age gradient is replicated in egg chromosome studies from a wide age range, so confounding is not a plausible explanation.
audit.newer_evidence: The trophectoderm-biopsy numbers are as stated [afert-franasiak2014], and direct study of egg chromosome segregation shows an age U-curve driven by cohesion loss [afert-gruhn2019].
audit.bottom_line: Nothing newer challenges this; age remains the single biggest factor in egg quality.

audit.claim: AMH and antral follicle count predict IVF egg yield but not natural fertility or egg quality.
audit.biases: Cohort studies are small for a modest effect (imprecision); the largest cohort was recruited from buyers of a commercial hormone test with self-reported pregnancy (selection, measurement error) and was run with company involvement [afert-nelson2024].
audit.newer_evidence: Follow-up of the Time to Conceive cohort (2023) found low AMH or high FSH unrelated to future live birth, infertility or fecundability [afert-harris2023], extending the 2017 null result [afert-steiner2017]. A 2024 cohort of 3150 women found a modest association (adjusted HR 0.77 for AMH <1 ng/mL; peak per-cycle conception 11% vs 14%) [afert-nelson2024]. A 2023 meta-analysis found AMH relates to cumulative IVF live birth without a threshold, and lacks data for natural conception [afert-peigne2023].
audit.bottom_line: A low AMH may slightly lower monthly chances, but most women with low AMH still conceive; it is not a fertility test.

site_change.note: Add Nelson 2024 (modest association, commercial cohort) and Harris 2023 (null, long follow-up) to the debate so readers see both sides.

audit.claim: Egg freezing works best young and with 10-15 eggs (~85% cumulative live birth at 35 or under), but only 9-38% of women return to use eggs.
audit.biases: Outcome data come from the minority who return (selection: returners differ in age and prognosis), single-centre series from leading clinics (the 85% figure), and models extrapolated from fresh IVF.
audit.newer_evidence: Two 2024 meta-analyses give pooled figures: about 11% of women return (median 7-year follow-up) and live birth per returning woman is about 28-29% [afert-hirsch2024, afert-kirubarajan2024]; 52% if eggs were frozen at 35 or younger and 19% at 40+ [afert-hirsch2024]. A large US clinic cohort found 43% cumulative live birth overall and over 70% only with 20+ mature eggs frozen before 38; extra freezing cycles did not independently help beyond the egg count [afert-cascante2024].
audit.bottom_line: The age and egg-number message holds, but pooled per-woman success is lower than the best single-clinic figures: roughly half at 35 or younger and one in five at 40+.

site_change.note: Alongside the 85% single-centre figure, give the pooled per-woman live birth (28% overall, 52% at <=35, 19% at >=40) and pooled return rate (~11%).

audit.claim: Most IVF add-ons do not raise live birth; HFEA gives no green rating for having a baby and ESHRE recommends little.
audit.biases: Add-on evidence is dominated by small trials, per-transfer reporting, industry funding and trustworthiness problems: in the intrauterine hCG field every trial that would not share data failed integrity checks and only those trials showed benefit [afert-zou2026]; similar patterns were found in PCOS trials [afert-bordewijk2020b].
audit.newer_evidence: The HFEA list reviewed 28 Sep 2026 still has no green rating for live birth (yellow for scratch, embryo glue and freeze-all; red for ERA, IVIG, steroids, PRP and PGT-A; black for time-lapse and PICSI) [afert-hfea2026]. ESHRE notes none of its 42 add-on recommendations rests on high-quality evidence [afert-eshre2023]. New RCTs since 2023 (prednisone, PGT-A in male factor, IPD of intrauterine hCG) were all null for live birth [afert-sun2023, afert-lin2025, afert-zou2026].
audit.bottom_line: The overview holds and has been reinforced by newer trials.

audit.claim: PGT-A does not raise live birth per woman and can lower it, while reducing miscarriage per transfer; HFEA red for live birth.
audit.biases: Per-transfer reporting (denominator selection) inflates apparent benefit; post hoc age subgroups; company-run studies on mosaic embryos.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 BMJ RCT in 450 couples with severe male factor found identical cumulative live birth (60.4% vs 60.9%) with fewer pregnancy losses (5.8% vs 19.1% after first transfer) [afert-lin2025], matching the 2021 NEJM trial (77.2% vs 81.8%) [afert-yan2021]. ASRM's 2024 committee opinion says routine PGT-A's value has not been demonstrated [afert-asrm2024pgta]. Supporters point to low-quality data in unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss suggesting more live births per patient [afert-mumusoglu2025] and a pilot RCT in women 35-42 with a non-significant cumulative gain (72% vs 52%, n=100) [afert-beebeejaun2025].
audit.bottom_line: Newer RCTs keep finding the same thing: fewer miscarriages, not more babies. A properly powered trial in older women and recurrent loss is still missing.

site_change.note: Add Lin 2025 BMJ RCT and the ASRM 2024 committee opinion; mention the open question for recurrent pregnancy loss (Mumusoglu 2025).

audit.claim: Hyaluronan transfer medium is the one add-on with a plausible live-birth gain (Cochrane RR 1.21), so ESHRE recommends it with single embryo transfer; HFEA amber.
audit.biases: Many older, small, industry-linked trials at high risk of bias; the benefit shrinks in low-risk-of-bias analyses [afert-heymann2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 meta-analysis of 24 RCTs found live birth RR 1.14 (0.99-1.31, not significant), shrinking to 1.06 (0.85-1.31) when high-risk-of-bias trials were excluded, and rated certainty very low [afert-rocha2026]. Cochrane 2020 still reports RR 1.21 at moderate certainty [afert-heymann2020]. The HFEA keeps it yellow/amber (unclear) [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Any gain is small and uncertain; it is cheap and probably harmless with single-embryo transfer, but not proven.

site_change.headline: Cochrane 2020 found about 21% more live births with hyaluronan transfer medium, but a 2026 meta-analysis found no significant gain (RR 1.14; 1.06 in low-bias trials); HFEA rates it amber and it raises twins if more than one embryo is transferred.

audit.claim: PIP found identical live birth; Cochrane 2026 calls the effect unclear (OR 1.12); several trials have had integrity questions.
audit.biases: Early positive trials were small and some came from groups whose work has since been retracted: two Egyptian scratch RCTs were retracted in 2024 [afert-maged2018, afert-helmy2017], within a wider pattern of integrity problems in women's-health trials from single institutes [afert-bordewijk2020a, afert-mol2024].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2026 restricted its primary analysis to low-risk-of-bias trials and found an unclear effect (OR 1.12, 0.98-1.28) [afert-perera2026]; the 1364-woman PIP trial found 26.1% live birth in both arms [afert-lensen2019]. HFEA yellow [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: At best a small benefit, judged now on trustworthy trials only.

site_change.note: Name the retracted trials (Maged 2018, Helmy 2017; retracted 2024) so readers know which early positive results to discount.

audit.claim: Receptivity-timed transfer gave no benefit in a 767-patient JAMA RCT; HFEA red, ESHRE not recommended.
audit.biases: The positive evidence is developer-run (per-protocol analysis with ~50% dropout) and observational meta-analyses with methodological errors [afert-wilkinson2024].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 8 studies found no live-birth difference (OR 1.38, 0.79-2.41) [afert-arian2023]; methodologists used ERA reviews as a case study of fatal flaws in observational meta-analyses [afert-wilkinson2024]. The JAMA RCT result stands (58.5% vs 61.9%) [afert-doyle2022]; HFEA red [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: No newer evidence supports receptivity testing.

audit.claim: TILT and SelecTIMO found no live-birth gain from time-lapse; HFEA black.
audit.biases: Earlier positive data were small or industry-sponsored; the large trials are independent and double-blind.
audit.newer_evidence: TILT (2024): live birth 33.7% time-lapse, 36.6% undisturbed culture, 33.0% standard [afert-bhide2024]. HFEA black [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

audit.claim: Assisted hatching made no clear live-birth difference (OR 1.09) and may raise multiples; HFEA grey.
audit.biases: Low-quality trials with publication bias.
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2021 conclusion unchanged [afert-lacey2021]; HFEA grey as of Sep 2026 [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

audit.claim: With normal semen, ICSI does not beat conventional IVF; reserve ICSI for male factor, prior fertilisation failure, PGT cycles or very few eggs.
audit.biases: Registry comparisons are confounded by indication; clinicians' belief that ICSI prevents total fertilisation failure drives use in poor-prognosis groups without trial support.
audit.newer_evidence: The Dang 2021 Lancet RCT stands (live birth 35% vs 31%, NS) [afert-dang2021]. A 2023 RCT in exactly the 'very few eggs / older women' group (age >=40 and/or <=4 oocytes, 336 cycles) found ICSI gave lower fertilisation (53% vs 62%) and no better live birth, and clearly worse results when both applied [afert-fancsovits2023].
audit.bottom_line: ICSI for normal sperm adds cost without benefit, including for older women and low egg numbers.

site_change.note: Remove 'very few eggs' (and advanced age) from the list of reasons to use ICSI, or flag that an RCT (Fancsovits 2023) found no benefit there.

audit.claim: No good evidence that immune testing or treatments help IVF; HFEA red for IVIG and steroids, grey for intralipids.
audit.biases: Positive data come from small or mixed-design studies (IVIG meta-analysis pooling case-control studies; a single 102-woman intralipid RCT).
audit.newer_evidence: A 715-woman JAMA RCT (2023) in recurrent implantation failure found prednisone did not raise live birth (37.8% vs 38.8%) and increased biochemical pregnancy loss (17.3% vs 9.9%) and preterm delivery (11.8% vs 5.5%) [afert-sun2023]. Cochrane remains uncertain for glucocorticoids (OR 1.37, 0.69-2.71) [afert-boomsma2022]. HFEA red for IVIG and steroids [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: The best trial of steroids found no benefit and signals of harm: avoid immune add-ons outside a trial.

site_change.headline: No good evidence that 'immune' tests or treatments help IVF: a 715-woman RCT found prednisone did not raise live birth and increased early loss and preterm birth; HFEA rates IVIG and steroids red and intralipids grey.
site_change.note: Add Sun 2023 (JAMA) to refs and debate.

audit.claim: Cochrane found a live-birth benefit only for day-3 transfers with >=500 IU and no evidence for blastocyst transfer; ESHRE does not recommend it.
audit.biases: The Cochrane subgroup benefit came from trials later found untrustworthy: in a 2026 IPD meta-analysis none of the trials that did not provide individual data met trustworthiness criteria, and those trials alone produced the positive effect [afert-zou2026]. This is a textbook example of research-integrity bias inflating a meta-analysis [afert-li2020].
audit.newer_evidence: IPD meta-analysis (2026) of 7 trustworthy RCTs, 2244 women: live birth OR 0.99 (0.83-1.19), clinical pregnancy OR 1.04; untrustworthy non-IPD trials showed OR 1.87 for pregnancy (P for interaction 0.005) [afert-zou2026]. Cochrane 2018 had rated the cleavage-stage subgroup moderate quality [afert-craciunas2018].
audit.bottom_line: Intrauterine hCG does not work; the apparent benefit came from unreliable trials.

site_change.headline: An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the 7 trustworthy RCTs (2244 women, 2026) found no effect on live birth (OR 0.99); the earlier 'benefit' came only from trials that failed integrity checks.
site_change.note: Replace the Cochrane 2018 subgroup framing as the lead finding.

audit.claim: Growth hormone adds about 1.4 eggs in poor responders; Cochrane suggests more live births at very low certainty; LIGHT was null; ESHRE does not recommend it.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials, mostly unblinded and from single centres; oocyte number is a surrogate.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 network meta-analysis of 22 RCTs (4131 poor responders) found no live-birth differences among hormonal add-ons, with GH ranked best only for oocyte numbers [afert-etrusco2025]. Cochrane 2021 and LIGHT stand [afert-sood2021, afert-norman2019].
audit.bottom_line: More eggs, no proven extra babies.

audit.claim: Cochrane 2024 (moderate certainty): DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders; testosterone looks more promising.
audit.biases: Research-integrity problems in the trial base: two DHEA RCTs in poor responders have been retracted, Elprince 2020 (retracted 2024) and Kotb 2016 (140 women, retracted 2026) [afert-elprince2020, afert-kotb2016, afert-kotb2016ret]; pooled estimates published before 2026 may contain such trials. Early small trials overstated benefit.
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2024 (28 RCTs): DHEA OR 1.30 (0.95-1.76); testosterone OR 2.53 [afert-naik2024]. A 2025 meta-analysis restricted to POSEIDON-defined low reserve found testosterone the only adjuvant linked to higher live birth (OR 2.19) [afert-conforti2025], while a 2025 network meta-analysis found no significant live-birth differences among hormonal add-ons [afert-etrusco2025]. HFEA rates androgens grey [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: DHEA does not reliably help; the testosterone signal is real enough to test properly but not established.

site_change.note: Debate field says 'None': add the retractions (Kotb 2016, Elprince 2020) and the testosterone-vs-DHEA contrast with HFEA grey.

audit.claim: Widely used in PCOS, but Cochrane rates the evidence very low and cannot show a live-birth benefit; one myo-inositol plus melatonin RCT was retracted in 2026.
audit.biases: Industry links and integrity: a second key trial, Papaleo 2009 (myo-inositol and oocyte quality in ICSI), was retracted in 2025 at the request of the ASRM Publications Committee for an undisclosed conflict of interest with the supplement maker [afert-papaleo2009, afert-papaleo2009ret], alongside the retracted Pacchiarotti 2016 trial [afert-pacchiarotti2016]. PCOS fertility trials that did not share data were more often at high risk of bias and gave different pooled results [afert-bordewijk2020b]. Cochrane's apparent miscarriage reduction rested on one trial with an unusually high control miscarriage rate [afert-showell2018].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis reports higher mature-egg rates in PCOS IVF but no data strong enough for live birth [afert-zhang2025]; Cochrane's live-birth estimate remains OR 2.42 (0.75-7.83) [afert-showell2018].
audit.bottom_line: There is still no reliable evidence that myo-inositol raises live birth, and two influential trials are now retracted.

site_change.note: Say 'two retractions' (Papaleo 2009 retracted 2025 for undisclosed COI; Pacchiarotti 2016) and cite the PCOS trial-integrity paper; debate field is 'None'.

audit.claim: Cochrane (63 trials) found only low to very low quality evidence; several included trials since retracted; ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in IVF.
audit.biases: Integrity: Cochrane's March 2026 editorial note lists 7 retracted and 2 'expression of concern' trials in the review; editors judge the main conclusion unchanged but the N-acetylcysteine vs L-carnitine comparison loses all data once El Sharkwy 2019 is removed [afert-showell2020, afert-elsharkwy2019]. Other retracted antioxidant fertility trials include CoQ10 with clomiphene in PCOS [afert-elrefaeey2014]. Trials are small, unregistered and use surrogate outcomes.
audit.newer_evidence: No large trustworthy RCT has since shown a live-birth gain. Cochrane-wide trustworthiness work shows such problems are common and are missed by Risk-of-Bias tools [afert-wilkinson2025].
audit.bottom_line: Be cautious: once retracted trials are removed, the evidence is weaker than the headline odds ratio suggests.

site_change.note: Debate field says 'None': add the 2026 editorial-note details and name El Sharkwy 2019 and El Refaeey 2014 as retracted.

audit.claim: In IVF RCTs melatonin raised clinical pregnancy (OR 1.43) and egg counts in low-quality data but not live birth.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials; a widely cited myo-inositol plus melatonin trial is retracted [afert-pacchiarotti2016]; live birth was reported by only 3 trials with low power [afert-hu2020].
audit.newer_evidence: No large live-birth RCT has appeared; the 2020 meta-analysis is still the main synthesis (live birth OR 1.38, 0.78-2.46, power 0.34) [afert-hu2020].
audit.bottom_line: Unproven for egg quality or live birth.

audit.claim: Moderate caffeine has little effect on conceiving; the clearer risk is miscarriage once pregnant, rising about 7% per 100 mg/day.
audit.biases: Reverse causation and confounding by the pregnancy signal: healthy pregnancies cause more nausea and food aversion, so women with viable pregnancies drink less coffee; smoking is a further confounder, and the source meta-analysis flags incomplete adjustment for both and possible publication bias [afert-chen2016]. One case-control study found the association survived adjustment for nausea [afert-giannelli2003].
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization, which avoids the nausea problem, found no effect of genetically predicted coffee drinking on pregnancy loss in UK Biobank and FinnGen (OR 0.96, 0.87-1.06), while the same method did detect harm from smoking (OR 1.31) [afert-yuan2021]; a 2023 MR and genetic-risk-score study likewise found no effect on miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth [afert-britonunes2023]. In the Norwegian MoBa cohort, triangulation with MR found consistent effects on time to conception only for smoking and BMI [afert-wootton2023]. Caveat: the MR instruments index habitual coffee intake in the general population, not caffeine dose in early pregnancy.
audit.bottom_line: Caffeine probably does little to fertility, and the miscarriage link may be largely confounded by pregnancy nausea; staying under about 200 mg/day in pregnancy remains a reasonable precaution, but the risk figure should not be read as causal.

site_change.headline: Moderate caffeine shows little or no effect on conceiving; cohort studies link high intake in pregnancy to miscarriage (about 7% per 100 mg/day), but this is likely partly confounded by pregnancy nausea, and two Mendelian randomization studies found no causal effect of coffee on miscarriage.
site_change.note: Fill the empty debate fields with Chen 2016 / Giannelli 2003 vs Yuan 2021 / Brito Nunes 2023.

audit.claim: PCOS carries systemic oxidative stress; fertility problems are mainly ovulatory; lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth.
audit.biases: Oxidative markers are cross-sectional and confounded by obesity and insulin resistance; weight-loss advice rests partly on observational data.
audit.newer_evidence: In obese women with PCOS, a secondary cross-trial comparison of two RCTs found lifestyle weight loss before clomiphene gave higher live birth (25% vs 10%) than immediate clomiphene [afert-legro2016]. In obese infertile women generally, the large LIFEstyle (NEJM 2016) and FIT-PLESE (2022) RCTs found no live-birth gain from preconception weight loss [afert-mutsaerts2016, afert-legro2022], and a 2024 meta-analysis found more pregnancies but not more live births (RR 1.19, 0.97-1.45) [afert-caldwell2024]. MR in MoBa supports a causal effect of higher BMI on longer time to conception [afert-wootton2023].
audit.bottom_line: Weight loss helps ovulation in PCOS, but randomised evidence that delaying treatment to lose weight raises live birth is weak outside PCOS-specific data.

site_change.note: The caveat 'Lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth' should mention Legro 2016 (live birth 25% vs 10%, non-randomised cross-trial comparison) and the null LIFEstyle and FIT-PLESE trials in obese infertile women.

audit.claim: Folic acid 400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects and is consistently associated with better fertility (15% higher fecundability, +20 points IVF live birth at >800 ug/day).
audit.biases: Fertility associations are observational and prone to healthy-user bias (supplement users plan pregnancies and have healthier habits).
audit.newer_evidence: The neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reaffirmed by USPSTF 2023 [afert-uspstf2023]. The only randomised fertility data come from the Hungarian periconceptional multivitamin trial (0.8 mg folic acid), which found more conceptions and more multiple births [afert-czeizel1994]. The EARTH IVF association remains a single cohort [afert-gaskins2014]. In men, folic acid plus zinc did not improve live birth (FAZST) [afert-schisterman2020].
audit.bottom_line: Take it for neural tube protection; any fertility gain is plausible but not proven and should not be presented as established.

site_change.note: Add Czeizel 1994 as the one randomised fertility signal and FAZST as the null male trial; label the 15%/20-point figures as observational.

audit.claim: Even mild iodine deficiency matters around conception: very low urinary iodine cut fecundability 46%, and mildly deficient UK mothers' children had higher odds of low verbal IQ (OR 1.58).
audit.biases: Measurement error (single spot urine for a nutrient that varies day to day, acknowledged by the authors) and residual confounding [afert-mills2018, afert-bath2013].
audit.newer_evidence: The only adequately powered RCT in mildly deficient pregnant women (832 women, 2017) found 200 ug/day iodine did not improve child IQ or executive function [afert-gowachirapant2017]; a 2020 meta-analysis found no cognitive effect in pooled RCTs and insufficient evidence for supplementation recommendations [afert-dineva2020]. A 2019 IPD meta-analysis of 6180 mother-child pairs found UI/Creat <150 ug/g not significantly linked to IQ, with a curvilinear verbal-IQ association limited to the first trimester [afert-levie2019]. The fecundability finding has not been replicated [afert-mills2018].
audit.bottom_line: Avoiding real deficiency is sensible (iodised salt, dairy, a prenatal with iodine), but trials have not shown that topping up mild deficiency improves children's IQ, and the fertility link is a single study.

site_change.headline: Mild iodine deficiency is linked in cohorts to slower conception and lower child verbal IQ, but a randomised trial of iodine in mildly deficient pregnant women found no IQ benefit; avoid deficiency rather than supplement high.
site_change.note: Add Gowachirapant 2017, Dineva 2020 and Levie 2019 to debate.

audit.claim: The EARTH 'profertility' diet was associated with 53% higher odds of IVF live birth per SD.
audit.biases: Score derived and tested in the same single cohort (overfitting), food-frequency measurement error, and healthy-user confounding among fertility-clinic patients.
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication of the profertility score has appeared. Meta-analyses of diet patterns in ART find all studies at moderate-high risk of bias, with Mediterranean and profertility patterns each associated with live birth in individual studies [afert-kellow2022, afert-winter2023]; in EARTH itself the Mediterranean benefit plateaued above the second quartile [afert-gaskins2019].
audit.bottom_line: A healthy diet is reasonable, but no specific 'fertility diet' has been shown to cause more live births.

site_change.note: Add Kellow 2022 and Winter 2023 meta-analyses to debate (field currently 'None').

audit.claim: Ejaculating every 1-2 days keeps SDF lower; a second sample 3 hours later cut SDF from 35% to 24%.
audit.biases: Most data are within-man before-after comparisons (regression to the mean when men are selected for high SDF) and small ART studies.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2024 dose-response meta-analysis of 85 studies found short abstinence lowered DFI modestly in healthy men (-2.4 points) [afert-du2024], and a 2023 meta-analysis linked a second ejaculate within 4 hours to higher ART live birth [afert-barbagallo2023]. The 2023 risk-factor meta-analysis found no significant SDF difference by abstinence period [afert-szabo2023].
audit.bottom_line: Short abstinence is cheap and probably helpful, with small average effects.

site_change.note: Debate field says 'None': add Szabo 2023 (no abstinence effect) vs Du 2024 and Barbagallo 2023.

audit.claim: A fever of 39-40 C for 2 days can raise DNA fragmentation and cut sperm count for 2-3 months before recovering.
audit.biases: Evidence is case reports and observational illness studies (the illness, medicines and weight loss travel with the fever).
audit.newer_evidence: The original case data stand [afert-sergerie2007]; a 2024 meta-analysis of COVID-19 found lower sperm concentration, count and motility during or soon after infection, mostly short-term [afert-cannarella2024].
audit.bottom_line: Holds; plan semen tests or ART about 3 months after a high fever where possible.

site_change.note: Add the COVID-19 meta-analysis to debate/refs.

audit.claim: Everyday heat raises scrotal temperature 1-3 C; boxer wearers have about 25% higher sperm concentration; SDF data thin.
audit.biases: Cross-sectional fertility-clinic data; underwear choice correlates with body size and lifestyle; self-report.
audit.newer_evidence: The underwear study itself found differences attenuated after adjustment for FSH, suggesting a compensatory pathway rather than pure confounding [afert-minguez2018]; no trial of changing underwear or laptop use has reported.
audit.bottom_line: Low-cost advice with plausible physiology; effect on fertility unproven.

audit.claim: Active infection and white cells in semen raise ROS and SDF; treating a proven infection can lower SDF by about a third.
audit.biases: The 'one third' fall comes from an uncontrolled before-after study [afert-gallegos2008]: men are selected for high SDF and abnormal tests, so some fall is expected from regression to the mean and spontaneous resolution.
audit.newer_evidence: The only RCT of antibiotics for leukocytospermia found frequent spontaneous resolution and no benefit of doxycycline or co-trimoxazole over no treatment [afert-yanushpolsky1995]. The 2023 SDF meta-analysis found Chlamydia and HPV effects on SDF negligible overall [afert-szabo2023].
audit.bottom_line: Treat a confirmed infection for its own sake, but do not expect a reliable SDF drop; leukocytes alone often clear without antibiotics.

site_change.headline: Active infection and white cells in semen are linked to higher ROS and SDF; one uncontrolled study saw SDF fall by a third after antibiotics, but the only RCT found leukocytospermia often resolves without them.
site_change.note: Add Yanushpolsky 1995 RCT.

audit.claim: Iron supplements were linked to less ovulatory infertility in NHS II, but newer cohorts found no consistent link; correct deficiency, extra iron does not help.
audit.biases: Healthy-user bias among supplement takers; self-reported intake.
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization found no causal effect of iron markers on infertility [afert-guo2024]. A Finnish before-after study reported more live births after IV iron in deficient women, but without a control group it is confounded by time and continued treatment [afert-tulenheimo2025]. Earlier cohorts as cited [afert-chavarro2006, afert-hahn2019].
audit.bottom_line: Correct iron deficiency, but don't take extra iron if your stores are normal.

site_change.note: Add Guo 2024 MR (null) and Tulenheimo-Silfvast 2025 (uncontrolled) to debate.

audit.claim: Endometriosis is pro-oxidant and linked to fewer eggs, but women with endometrioma have similar IVF live birth (OR 0.98); surgery before IVF did not help.
audit.biases: Mostly retrospective comparisons; egg-quality claims rest on small biological studies.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2021 meta-analysis again found fewer oocytes but similar live birth with endometrioma [afert-alshehre2021], consistent with the 2015 review [afert-hamdan2015].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

site_change.note: Debate field says 'None'; add Alshehre 2021 as confirmation.

audit.claim: Large RCTs found vitamin C 1000 mg + E 400 IU did not prevent pre-eclampsia and raised some harms.
audit.biases: Not applicable; the claim rests on large RCTs.
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analysis of 9 trials (19,810 women) confirms RR 1.00 for pre-eclampsia with more gestational hypertension and membrane rupture [afert-condeagudelo2011].
audit.bottom_line: Holds: a textbook case of RCTs overturning the antioxidant hypothesis.

audit.claim: In high-risk pregnancies aspirin 150 mg nightly cut preterm pre-eclampsia from 4.3% to 1.6%; USPSTF recommends 81 mg.
audit.biases: Not applicable; RCT and IPD evidence.
audit.newer_evidence: ASPRE and the Cochrane IPD-based review stand [afert-rolnik2017, afert-duley2019]; the 75 vs 150 mg dose question remains under trial.
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

audit.claim: Pooled small trials suggest benefit but the only low-risk trial was null; HFEA red.
audit.biases: High-risk-of-bias trials drive the pooled effect.
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2024 and HFEA as cited [afert-vaidakis2024, afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

audit.claim: Two RCTs in poor responders found no gain in euploid embryos; HFEA red.
audit.biases: Supporting data are uncontrolled case series.
audit.newer_evidence: PROVA RCT null [afert-herlihy2024]; Cochrane very low certainty [afert-vaidakis2024].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

audit.claim: Selecting 'better' sperm lowers SDF in the dish but has not raised live birth; HFEA PICSI black, SDF-guided selection grey.
audit.biases: Small single-centre positive trials; surrogate outcome (DFI of prepared sample).
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2026: hyaluronan selection may make little difference to live birth (RR 1.09) and probably reduces miscarriage [afert-garg2026]; HABSelect null [afert-miller2019]. On the other side, an Egyptian 4-arm RCT in high-SDF couples reported higher ongoing pregnancy with PICSI and MACS than density-gradient preparation [afert-hozyen2022].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

site_change.note: Hozyen 2022 could be added as the main positive RCT in high-SDF couples (single centre).
